words.gram: preposition governing prepositional or accusative case

lines.trans: Whatever you cook is what we will eat.
I am just really tired today.
Listen, why don't we order something?
Maybe let's make some quick pancakes, huh?

meanings.note: Everyday conversational Russian interj meaning 'hi', frequent in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Dima, hi. What are you doing?
Hi there. Are you hungry?
Say hello to Dad, we will call.

meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (root 'голодаться'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to get hungry', forming an aspectual pair with 'голодать'.

examples.trans: Hi there. Are you hungry?
The guests became very hungry.
After the walk we were hungry.

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('well') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or negation in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Can you show a little respect for my hard work?
Vika, come on, don't be angry.
Well, we will find somebody.

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to be'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.trans: You need to act more natural, understand?
I will not distract you.

examples.text: Мой карьерный рост был долгим и трудным.
examples.trans: My career climb was long and difficult.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'a little'.

examples.trans: I need to do a bit of work.
I'm a bit tired.

examples.text: Мы даём вам ещё немного времени.
examples.trans: We are giving you a little more time.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('what') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.trans: Am I talking to a wall?
What? Excuse me.
Vitya, what is going on here, pal?

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'at' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.trans: We have an ideal family.

examples.text: У нас разве не все гости побывали?
examples.trans: Haven't all the important guests visited us already?
Our deadlines are burning.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('we') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.trans: We recently returned from Paris.

examples.text: Мы вернулись в Россию и поженились.
examples.trans: We returned to Russia and got married.
We have an ideal family.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'today'.

examples.trans: I have that important guest today, remember?
Tonight she is definitely going to cook.

examples.text: Дмитрий Владимирович, вы же сегодня на съёмках?
examples.trans: Dmitry Vladimirovich, aren't you at a shoot today?

meanings.note: Russian preposition meaning 'on' that governs a specific oblique case on the following noun phrase.

examples.text: Тебе это на канал не пропустят.
examples.trans: They will not let that on television.
For a couple of days.
Set a reminder on your phone.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'dinner', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.text: Что у нас сегодня на ужин?
examples.trans: What do we have for dinner tonight?
A romantic dinner for two.

examples.text: Кстати, звонили из итальянского ресторана. Дарят папе романтический ужин на двоих.
examples.trans: By the way, they called from the Italian restaurant. They're giving Dad a romantic dinner for two.

приготовить.gloss: to prepare, to cook, to make

meanings.en: to prepare, to cook, to make
meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (root 'готовить'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to prepare', forming an aspectual pair with 'готовить'.

examples.trans: Will you cook something, huh?
Of course I will cook.

examples.text: Что приготовишь, то и будем есть.
examples.trans: Whatever you cook is what we will eat.

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'otherwise', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.

examples.text: А то мы уже начали беспокоиться.
examples.trans: We were starting to worry, you see.
Faster, or we'll be late.

examples.text: Это хорошо, что готово. А то мы уже начали беспокоиться.
examples.trans: It's good that it's ready. We were starting to worry.

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'and', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Мы вернулись в Россию и поженились.
examples.trans: We returned to Russia and got married.

examples.text: Мой карьерный рост был долгим и трудным.
examples.trans: My career climb was long and difficult.

examples.text: Я готовил для президентов России и Франции.
examples.trans: I cooked for the presidents of Russia and France.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('I') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.trans: I still work as a cook.
I finally proposed to Vika.

examples.text: Вика! Ты вообще меня не слушаешь?
examples.trans: Wait, are you not listening to me at all?

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'can', forming an aspectual pair with 'смочь'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.text: Виктор Петрович, мы не можем долго ждать.
examples.trans: Viktor Petrovich, we cannot wait that long.
We can start filming now.

examples.text: Сказал, что продюсер на месте, можешь подавать блюда.
examples.trans: He said the producer is at his table and you can serve the dishes.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'of course'.

examples.trans: Of course I remember.
Of course I will cook.
I can cook, of course.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'just'.

examples.trans: It looks simply incredible.
I am just really tired today.
Ridiculous. He is just a clown.

meanings.note: Prefix 'у-' marks departure, removal, or successful completion (root 'стать'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to get tired', forming an aspectual pair with 'уставать'.

examples.trans: I am just really tired today.
I am very tired of sitting.
She is tired after work.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (root 'лушать'). Used in Russian as an imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to listen', forming an aspectual pair with 'послушать'.

examples.text: Вика! Ты вообще меня не слушаешь?
examples.trans: Wait, are you not listening to me at all?
Listen to me very carefully now.

examples.text: Слушай, Вика мне никогда не пекла блинов.
examples.trans: Listen, Vika has never baked pancakes for me.

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('let's') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or negation in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Let's clean up!
See you, bye!
Arkasha, let's clean up!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('something') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.trans: Will you cook something, huh?
Listen, why don't we order something?
Say something.

meanings.note: Prefix 'за-' marks beginning an action, covering, or stopping by along the way (root 'казать'). Used in Russian as an perfective verb focusing on a single completed action or result meaning 'to order', forming an aspectual pair with 'заказывать'.

examples.trans: Listen, why don't we order something?
Maybe we should order?
We ordered tea and sandwiches.

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('maybe') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or negation in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Maybe you could help?
Maybe tomorrow.
I thought maybe you wouldn't see me.

meanings.note: Declinable masculine noun meaning 'pancake', changing its case ending across all six Russian grammatical cases to mark its role in the clause.

examples.trans: Maybe let's make some quick pancakes, huh?
Why pancakes of all things?

examples.text: Во-первых, мама блинчиков для вас испекла.
examples.trans: First, Mom baked pancakes for you.

meanings.note: Invariable Russian adverb used to modify verbs or whole clauses with the sense 'quickly'.

examples.trans: Let us grab a bite quickly.
Doing this in a hurry will not work.

examples.text: По-быстрому такой нож купить не получится.
examples.trans: You can't buy such a knife in a hurry.

meanings.note: Coordinating or subordinating Russian conjunction meaning 'and', linking clauses in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Vitya, what is going on here, pal?
Ah, that too.
Will you cook something, huh?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronoun ('you') that declines for case depending on its grammatical function in the sentence.

examples.text: Вика! Ты вообще меня не слушаешь?
examples.trans: Wait, are you not listening to me at all?

examples.text: Или я для тебя пустое место?
examples.trans: Or am I invisible to you?
Vika, did you want to say something?

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('but') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or negation in spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Does that really happen?

examples.text: Я же сказал, договорюсь с Нагиевым.
examples.trans: I told you, I will make a deal with Nagiyev.

examples.text: Я же тебя просила не бриться моим станком.
examples.trans: I asked you not to shave with my razor.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'excellently'.

examples.trans: Now that looks great.
Now it is filmed. Excellent.
I can. Great.

meanings.note: Conversational Russian particle ('here') that adds modal nuance, emphasis, or negation in spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Вот тут передачу про меня снимают.
examples.trans: They are filming a show about me right here.
Now that looks great.
Now it is filmed. Excellent.

meanings.note: Russian determiner/pronoun ('all') agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun phrase it specifies.

examples.text: У нас разве не все гости побывали?
examples.trans: Haven't all the important guests visited us already?
No, not all of them wanted this.

examples.text: Меня не будет, я весь день на съёмках.
examples.trans: I won't be here, I'm at a shoot all day.

meanings.note: Descriptive Russian adjective meaning 'ready', agreeing in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies.

examples.trans: My guest is ready and waiting!

examples.text: Я для вас готов быть официантом.
examples.trans: For you I am ready to be a waiter myself.
Here, everything is ready.

meanings.note: Russian imperfective verb expressing ongoing, habitual, or repeated action meaning 'to smell'; conjugates for person and number in the present/future and agrees in gender in the past tense.

examples.trans: It smells delicious.
It smells bad here.
The coffee smells good.

meanings.note: Manner or predicative adverb in '-о' derived from the corresponding adjective stem, used in everyday speech to mean 'tasty'.

examples.trans: I am sure all of this is very tasty.
It smells delicious.
It's delicious!
